site.name: Abhinav Pangaria
site.longBio: Engineer who takes a problem down to the primitive it is missing and builds that. Orchestration and verification harnesses that make an autonomous agent prove its work rather than report it. Cryptographic systems that stop a public ledger from naming who paid whom. Settlement backends where a retry is theft and there is nothing to roll back. Retrieval and data pipelines inside a bank's asset and wealth management division, where the bottleneck was never the model. Rust, Go, Python and TypeScript across five runtimes, most of it owned end to end from the contract up to the dashboard.
site.headline: I build resilient systems, from idea to production.
site.heroLine: Full-stack engineer across backend, infrastructure and the product on top. Previously JP Morgan Chase. Stellar SCF grantee.

about.lead: I build things end to end: the idea, the system underneath it, and the part people actually touch.
about.body: The subject keeps changing. So far it has been developer tools, payments, privacy, language learning and research, sometimes alone and sometimes inside a large bank. The habit stays the same: understand the problem properly, build the smallest thing that really solves it, then keep at it until it holds up with real people using it.

projects.name: Sieve
projects.tagline: A vector search engine written from scratch in Rust: a billion vectors, searched on one laptop.
projects.description: A from-scratch Rust implementation of the search pipeline Exa described in How we built a web-scale vector database: Matryoshka 256-d prefixes, 1-bit codes scored against a float query with NEON lookup tables, IVF routing, then a rerank. Measuring it against exact search and NIST relevance labels showed routing, not the codes, was losing recall, so each vector is also spilled into a second cluster (SOAR), and RaBitQ residual codes replace the global ones. A three-tier store keeps 1-bit and 2-bit codes in RAM and reads int8 rerank rows from SSD with parallel pread, so 87 GB of rerank vectors never have to fit in memory. On the full TREC-RAG 2024 corpus of 113.5M passages it serves R@10 0.909 at 4.8 ms p50 on one 24 GB laptop, or R@10 0.902 in 225 MB of RAM with everything on SSD. On 1 billion vectors (SPACEV-1B) the same laptop builds an index in about 22 minutes and serves R@10 0.906 at 420 QPS. It also shards with a two-phase merge, takes live inserts and deletes with a write-ahead log, and runs filtered and hybrid BM25 search.

projects.name: Voluntas
projects.tagline: A Rust order-book collector for Kalshi and Polymarket that keeps every book exact.
projects.description: A take-home challenge, written up in full. The service subscribes to every live market on a prediction-market exchange, keeps an L2 order book for each one, and writes every price-level change to stdout plus a snapshot of every book once a minute, in the challenge's aligned SBE format. One engine runs both venues; only the websocket encode and decode layer changes. On AWS (c7i.xlarge, London) it held about 550k Polymarket tokens for an hour at 41k to 43k updates/s, and a two-hour run the next day replayed 118.2M snapshots from the deltas with 0 mismatches, at 1.97 GB peak memory and a load of 1.1 of 4 vCPU. Kalshi ran its whole demo universe from Virginia for two hours: 32.3M updates, 48.9M snapshots replayed, 0 mismatches. A single demo script builds it, replays a committed capture, runs every test against mock venues, and collects live markets.

projects.name: Prefill and the Frame
projects.tagline: Local inference vs. the browser compositor: why GPU-heavy pages stutter while a model reads.
projects.description: Independent research on one sentence from Dart's DBR-2026-05: a model that starves the compositor makes a janky browser. On a MacBook Pro (M4 Pro, 24 GB) a harness records every page frame next to every inference phase on one clock, 717 trials stored in SQLite. While a local 7B model prefills a 4k-token prompt at llama.cpp's default batch of 512, a GPU-heavy page drops 64% of its frames; decode drops about 0%, and CPU-only inference drops 0.1%, so the GPU is the shared resource. Capping the prefill batch at 64 tokens takes that page to 1.3% (WebGL Aquarium from 83% to 0%) for 9 to 11% more time to first token, with a 3B or 7B model. Safari shows the same mechanism. The fix does not carry over to 14B, still 31% at batch 64, which suggests a base M1 or M2 running 7B behaves the same way. It also reruns Dart's published TTFT and memory claims, and lays out what I would do next.

projects.name: Loom
projects.tagline: A shared, live world model for parallel coding agents, kept in one graph.
projects.description: Parallel AI coding agents write code that passes alone and breaks when merged. Agent A changes a function's contract, agent B writes a new caller against the old one, git sees no conflict, and the tests fail only after the merge. Loom keeps the code's call graph, every agent's in-flight edits, function-level leases, decisions and test evidence in one FalkorDB graph. On every edit a CALLS traversal of one to three hops finds exactly the agents whose in-flight code depends on the change, and Loom tells them what changed under them, mid-work. Leases are an atomic Cypher compare-and-set: 50 agents making 10,000 attempts got zero double grants, against 2,332 with the check disabled. Test runs are tied to the body hash they ran against, so a later edit marks a claim stale and blocks it, and any symbol can be walked back through decision, task, agent, change and commit. Measured on the 36 STALE-bench Django task pairs with Claude Haiku, 108 real runs across blind, oracle and live: without Loom 0 of 36 merges passed, with Loom 24 of 36 did, including 12 of 12 signature changes. Most of the remaining failures are return-type changes, where the notice arrived and the model kept its own code anyway.

projects.name: Guardian Kane
projects.tagline: The loop that makes an agent's "done" something it has to prove, not just say.
projects.description: Guardian Kane is a reviewed, phased, scope-guarded verification loop wrapped around Claude Code, not just a Stop-hook check (that's where it started; the current build spans twelve numbered phases). Every PRD use-case and generated test has to clear a review gate before it counts as real. A phased task tracker attributes every task, claim, and file to a build phase. Per-task verification then drives a real local browser through a scripted test plus an independent defect sweep before a task can advance to KANE_VERIFIED. Three failed attempts escalate to a human instead of looping forever. Underneath that: a local Jaccard-similarity bug-memory store, a real-time scope guard, a secret-scan security gate, file-level task locking, and a four-tab dashboard (code graph, memory graph, PRD graph with gaps & drift, live activity) with a chat bridge straight into the running agent. Proven across four paired A/B builds, including the flagship ORBITAL financial dashboard, where the unassisted baseline reported "done" on a doubled chart and an off-spec alerts layout, and the gated build shipped neither.

projects.name: AgentOps
projects.tagline: The organizational control plane for agents that hold money.
projects.description: A wallet gives an agent the ability to pay. AgentOps decides whether it is allowed to. Every agent is an explicit organizational identity with its own wallet, role, policy bindings and budget, and every economic action it attempts runs one fail-closed path: verify identity, evaluate policy, check budget, escalate to a human when a threshold is crossed, then execute, settle, and write an evidence record that links the agent's intent to its on-chain settlement. Money moves on Circle's infrastructure, with the rail chosen by the relationship: x402 and Gateway for machine-to-service commerce, Permit2 for bounded agent-to-agent spending, ERC-8183 escrow for a first interaction with an unproven counterparty, and ERC-8004 identity and reputation once the work completes. Agents reach the control plane over a hosted MCP server, the same one human operators govern. Demonstrated as a five-agent research organization across Arc Testnet and Base Sepolia: policy-controlled hiring, second-hop delegation where an agent hires another agent on its own authority, approval-gated cross-chain execution, and capital that can be revoked from an agent and recovered.

projects.name: Zidd
projects.tagline: An AI English coach for learners in India, from Class 2 chapters to the interview room.
projects.description: Zidd is an AI English coach built for learners in India, and it runs two products on one engine. School teaches NCERT-aligned English for Classes 2 to 5 across 47 authored chapters, with a placement diagnostic, teaching sessions, recaps, and reports a parent can read. Career runs communication drills, mock interviews and group-discussion simulations for job-seekers. Learners answer in their own words, with explanations in English, Hinglish or Hindi. Every answer goes through a LangGraph decision graph that scores it and picks the next teaching move: teach a new idea, bridge down when the learner is lost, strengthen, challenge once they have it, or redirect when the answer is fluent but off the question. Every loop is capped so nobody gets drilled forever, and progression runs on a streak of clean passes rather than a moving average, because an average that settles at 0.8 never crosses a strict 0.8 gate and soft-locks a learner who is getting it right. The reply streams token by token over SSE. Underneath, it is built to stay correct on a free tier: boot fails closed if the secret, database or schema is wrong, open-answer grading runs through a Postgres job queue that resumes after a crash, session starts and credit charges carry idempotency keys so a retry never double-charges, and a pool of Gemini keys rotates on rate limits. Reports only state progress the saved evidence supports, so an empty report says so instead of guessing.

projects.name: Pods
projects.tagline: NIM-backed accountability for small groups. Commit, show up, earn, repeat.
projects.description: Pods is a NIM-backed accountability app for small groups on Nimiq Pay. Commit NIM upfront, submit proof for scheduled activities like shipping code, fitness, reading, or study, and get payouts proportional to your presence. The creator reviews proof but never funds or receives participant money, so every settlement stays deterministic and disclosed.

projects.name: VEIL
projects.tagline: Privacy as a wallet primitive. Shielded notes, private sends, and prediction markets on Stellar.
projects.description: A private wallet and prediction market built on Stellar testnet. Public USDC converts into spendable shielded notes, private note-to-note transfers, batch payouts, and market participation all run through the same note model, so privacy is part of the wallet flow rather than bolted on. A backend prover and relayer generate proofs, simulate transactions, and settle pool state on-chain.

projects.name: Kredio
projects.tagline: DeFi with memory. Polkadot's on-chain credit layer.
projects.description: A credit layer for Polkadot that scores a borrower from on-chain behaviour rather than an oracle feed, so there is no price or reputation input to manipulate and nothing to bribe. Scoring runs across two runtimes at once through hybrid EVM and PolkaVM atomic calls, and the resulting score travels between parachains over XCM, which means a borrower's history follows them instead of restarting on every chain.

projects.name: OpenAssets
projects.tagline: The Mantle-native gateway bridging the RWA liquidity gap.
projects.description: A fundamental Real-World Asset (RWA) execution layer. Built for the Mantle Global Hackathon, OpenAssets transforms off-chain cash flows into credit-enabled primitives. Featuring ERC-3643 (T-REX) compliance, mETH-powered leverage vaults, and 'Token-Day' engines to prevent yield sniping. A system built for the next cycle of institutional RealFi.

projects.name: PayZoll
projects.tagline: Cross-border payroll and treasury, built for crypto-native teams.
projects.description: Cross-border payroll and treasury for teams whose members all hold different assets. I was sole technical owner of the payment infrastructure on a two-person founding team. The Stellar Disbursement Platform went from single-tenant to a multi-tenant distributed system running batch payroll for many organizations at once, with signing keys derived in AWS KMS instead of stored as raw tokens and payroll records encrypted at rest with pgcrypto. The interesting constraint was throughput: SDP was capped at eight channel accounts, roughly two transactions per second. Soroban's authorization-tree model let a single channel account fan out into many parallel contract calls, which took it to about 200.

projects.name: Tesseract
projects.tagline: Privacy-preserving payment & identity mixing on Stellar.
projects.description: Deposit, wait, withdraw. Built to expand Stellar Disbursement Platform with Privacy, Tesseract severs the link between depositor and recipient. Featuring channel-account rotation and layered hybrid encryption, it ensures that the most boring path through the system is also the most private one.
